analysis.one_liner: Makes large factory farms pay disaster and cleanup costs, bans cruel mass-killing methods, and protects meat plant workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made large industrial livestock operators liable for disaster cull costs and worker protections, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted large industrial animal farms — those housing at least 2,500 hogs or roughly 82,000 chickens. It would have required them to register disaster plans with the Department of Agriculture, pay annual fees, and cover the full costs of mass animal culls and disasters, instead of leaving those costs to taxpayers, workers, and neighbors. It banned cruel mass-killing methods like ventilation shutdown and sodium nitrite poisoning, gave cull workers severance, health coverage, and whistleblower protections, banned the use of incarcerated labor in culls, and rolled back faster slaughter-line speeds and industry self-inspection. It also extended humane slaughter rules to poultry and barred the sale of meat from downed livestock.
analysis.who_benefits: Slaughterhouse and poultry plant workers, who get severance, health coverage, and whistleblower protections during mass culls; contract farmers, who get lost-revenue compensation if an integrator cancels their contract after a disaster; people living near large feeding operations, who can sue for property and health damage; taxpayers, who currently absorb the cost of disaster culls and cleanup; and consumers and farmed animals, through humane-slaughter and inspection reforms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Plant workers, contract growers, farm neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Workers who perform depopulation — the mass killing of animals during disasters — would get 12 weeks of severance if fired within 60 days of the event, an employer-paid silver-level health plan for at least two years, and whistleblower protection, enforced by the Department of Labor with a private right of action [S3].
Contract growers whose contracts are terminated after a disaster would receive compensation equal to their revenue from the integrator over the preceding 180 days [S3].

Covered operators would be liable for disaster and depopulation costs, including health impacts and property losses suffered by neighboring residents, shifting costs that previously fell on taxpayers and communities [S3].

The bill bans depopulation by sodium nitrite poisoning, ventilation shutdown, and water-based foaming, with penalties up to $1,000 per animal, and requires depopulation methods that rapidly induce unconsciousness with minimal pain [S3].

It terminates slaughter programs that allow line speeds beyond existing limits or replace federal inspectors with company employees, and funds additional OSHA and Food Safety and Inspection Service inspectors [S3].

It includes poultry under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act — federal humane slaughter law currently covers only about 2 percent of food animals — and bans slaughtering or selling nonambulatory livestock [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large industrial livestock operators — big hog, turkey, and chicken operations and the meatpackers behind them — who would pay annual fees of at least $1 per animal, annual disaster mitigation costs, full liability for culls and cleanup, severance and two years of employer-paid health coverage for cull workers, and penalties up to $1,000 per animal for banned killing methods.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall on large operators, but those costs are typically passed through the supply chain; meat prices for consumers, or payments to contract growers, could rise [S3].

Operators may argue that in a true emergency — a barn fire, a fast-moving disease outbreak — the banned methods are sometimes the only workable option at scale, and humane alternatives like controlled-atmosphere stunning require equipment many facilities do not have; the bill appropriates $750 million to help poultry plants transition but capacity would take years to build [S3].

The two-year employer-paid health coverage mandate and 12-week severance apply regardless of employment or contract status, a cost that honest supporters would acknowledge is substantial and applies even to workers engaged briefly during a cull [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts real, documented costs — disaster culls that killed over 70 million animals since 2019, cleanup, worker harm, and taxpayer bailouts — onto the large operators that create them, and it gives workers and neighbors enforceable rights. The costs are real but aimed at operators with record profits, including 300 percent profit growth during the pandemic, per the bill's own findings. The main design risk is transition capacity: banning certain cull and transport practices without enough humane alternative infrastructure could strain producers in emergencies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on November 29, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1].
No cosponsors joined from either party [S4].
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a companion House bill, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large industrial livestock operators and meatpackers are better off: they avoided annual fees, disaster-cost liability, worker protection mandates, depopulation penalties, and the end of high-speed slaughter and self-inspection programs. Taxpayers continue to absorb disaster cull costs, and plant workers and neighboring communities remain without the protections the bill would have created.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Agriculture Committee; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (18th chair: Sen. Debbie Stabenow, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock operators and meatpackers (large hog, poultry, and turkey integrators)
industries.note: These operators would pay annual fees of at least $1 per animal, full liability for disaster and depopulation costs including neighbors' damages, severance and two years of employer-paid health coverage for cull workers, and penalties up to $1,000 per animal for banned cull methods. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against workers, rural neighbors, and taxpayers, who currently absorb those costs.

Growers raising animals under contract for integrators would receive lost-revenue compensation equal to 180 days of revenue if their contract is terminated after a disaster event, and whistleblower protection.

A $750 million grant program would help smaller poultry plants transition to controlled-atmosphere stunning, and a pilot program would expand no-cost inspection access — measures the bill frames as creating a level playing field in what its findings call a highly monopolized market.
The bill bans using these growth-promotion drugs in healthy livestock, a market the pharmaceutical industry would lose; the bill links the drugs to animals becoming nonambulatory.
Operators using incarcerated workers for depopulation labor would lose federal contracts and federal inspection eligibility for 10 years, ending a source of cheap disaster-cull labor.
